blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is the better choice for raw residential proxies: $35 for 10 GB against about $53 at Nimble's docs rate, roughly $200 for 100 GB against $530, and traffic that never expires. Neither offers SOCKS5 on residential, so protocol support does not separate them. Nimble is the better option only if you want AI-driven browsing, search agents and structured data delivered rather than proxies to run yourself. For in-house scraping teams, Rayobyte is the far cheaper path.

Rayobyte and Nimble both sell residential proxies and scraping tools, but they approach the market from opposite directions. Rayobyte is a cost-focused proxy vendor with non-expiring residential traffic that drops to $0.90/GB at volume, plus Web Unblocker and Scraping Robot. Nimble (Nimbleway) is an AI-first data platform that charges premium per-GB rates and leads with its Nimble Browser and managed data pipelines. This comparison helps you decide between cheap bandwidth and a managed data layer.

blocks.text: Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte combines one of the strongest datacenter proxy catalogs with a simple residential offer. Residential traffic is bought in volume bands, from $3.50/GB below 50 GB down to $0.90/GB at a terabyte, and it never expires. Users often praise its human support team. The trade-offs are HTTP-only residential access and limited public data on pool size.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Nimble in 2026: what you get

Nimble (Nimbleway) is an AI-first web-data platform. It offers residential proxies with fast response times and unlimited concurrency, but most of its product investment goes into the Nimble Browser, SERP and e-commerce APIs, and data-services plans that start in the thousands of dollars per month. It does not disclose its residential pool size, and its per-GB rates are among the highest here, so it competes on finished results rather than cheap traffic.

Strengths: Strong managed APIs and an AI-driven browser; Unlimited concurrency on proxies; Credits shared across all Nimble products; Free 5,000-page API trial. Weak spots: No published pool size; HTTP/HTTPS only, no SOCKS5 on proxies; High per-GB price for raw residential traffic.
Pricing: Rayobyte vs Nimble
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

Nimble's plan cards list residential proxy traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go, falling through credit packages ($150 and $600 entry packages) toward $5.30/GB; its current developer documentation lists $5.30/GB for residential traffic without a commitment. Annual billing saves 15%. Its scraping APIs bill $0.90 to $1.45 per 1,000 URLs depending on rendering.

At 10 GB a month, Rayobyte is the cheaper option at about $35 against $53 for Nimble, roughly 34% less. At 100 GB a month, Rayobyte is the cheaper option at about $200 against $530 for Nimble, roughly 62% less. The sticker price is only half of it. Rayobyte's unused traffic carries forward, while Nimble's does not (credits usable across nimble products), so if your usage swings from month to month Rayobyte can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte and Nimble do not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published' and Nimble lists 'Not published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Rayobyte lists Global countries and Nimble lists Worldwide. On targeting, Rayobyte offers country, region and city, while Nimble offers country, state and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Neither provider offers SOCKS5 on its residential gateway, so both are limited to HTTP(S) traffic. On sessions, Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available, and Nimble offers auto-rotation by default; sticky sessions available. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. Nimble: its managed APIs remove much of the anti-bot work. Let price and the countries you need decide.

SERP and rank tracking: Nimble wins. The deciding factor for Nimble: its SERP API and search agents return structured results. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: usable, with no dedicated SERP product.

Social media and multi-account management: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools. How Nimble compares: no SOCKS5 and a high per-GB cost make it a poor fit for account work.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. Nimble: dedicated e-commerce data APIs. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Ad verification and geo-testing: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Rayobyte: fewer carrier or ASN controls. With Nimble: good geo targeting but no published pool data. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Tight budgets: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. How Nimble compares: per-GB rates are among the highest here.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Nimble: Free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs. Verification and payment rules differ too. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Nimble: Sales-led onboarding for data-services plans. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Rayobyte and Nimble before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Rayobyte vs Nimble faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Rayobyte: check current offer; Nimble: free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Rayobyte comes out ahead in 2, Nimble in 1, and 3 are ties. That makes Rayobyte the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget, while Nimble is strongest for teams that want structured data rather than raw IPs. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.

AI and agent workloads that need a managed browser
Buyers comfortable with sales-led contracts
